purpose: Rufinamide is used to help control seizures in people with a rare and severe condition called Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, which usually starts in childhood. It is typically used along with other seizure medications, not on its own. It can help reduce how often seizures happen.
how_it_works: Rufinamide works by calming down overactive electrical signals in the brain that cause seizures. It does this by slowing down certain channels in nerve cells that carry electrical messages, which helps prevent those signals from firing too fast or too often. Think of it like putting a speed limit on runaway electrical activity in the brain.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include sleepiness or drowsiness, headache, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, decreased appetite, and fatigue. Some people may also have double vision or trouble walking steadily. These effects are often mild and may improve as your body adjusts to the medication.
warnings: Do not stop taking this medication suddenly without talking to your doctor, as this can cause more seizures. Tell your doctor if you have a heart condition called 'short QT syndrome' because rufinamide can affect your heart rhythm. It may also cause serious skin reactions or allergic reactions — seek medical help right away if you develop a rash, fever, or swollen lymph nodes. This medication can cause suicidal thoughts in some people, so let your doctor know right away if you feel depressed or have unusual mood changes.
typical_dosing: Rufinamide is taken by mouth as a tablet or liquid, usually twice a day with food. The dose depends on your weight and other medications you are taking. Your doctor will start you on a low dose and slowly increase it over time to find the right amount for you. Always take it exactly as your doctor prescribes.
